sections.skill: Build a balanced monthly budget from net income and adjust it

questions.prompt: What is a budget?

choices.text: A plan for how income will be used
A list of the bills you already paid last year
A type of savings account with a fixed rate
A bank's limit on how much you may spend

questions.correct_answer: A plan for how income will be used
questions.intro: A budget is a plan for your money: it lists expected income and assigns it to expenses, savings, and goals for a period, usually a month. A budget is "balanced" when planned spending and saving equal income.
questions.feedback: A budget plans how income will be spent and saved.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a plan with a record of the past
misconceptions.C: Confuses a plan with an account

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Nia's monthly take-home pay is $1,980. Her planned expenses total $2,115. What does her budget show?

choices.text: A $135 surplus
A $4,095 surplus
A balanced budget
A $135 deficit

questions.intro: Budget result = income − planned expenses. Positive: surplus (money left to save or use). Negative: deficit (planned spending is more than income), which must be fixed by earning more or spending less.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: In a zero-based budget, income minus all planned spending and saving equals zero. Ty earns $2,400. He plans $1,850 for expenses and $300 for savings. How much is left to assign?
questions.intro: A zero-based budget gives every dollar a job: expenses, savings, debt payments, or goals. Money is not "left over"; any unassigned money gets a purpose.
questions.feedback: $2,400 − $1,850 − $300 = $250 to assign, for example to an emergency fund.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Nia must close a $135 monthly deficit. Which change is MOST realistic and keeps her needs covered?

choices.text: Cut takeout by $80 and pause a $55 subscription
Stop paying her electric bill for a month
Use a credit card to cover the $135 gap every month
Skip her car insurance payment

questions.correct_answer: Cut takeout by $80 and pause a $55 subscription
questions.feedback: $80 + $55 = $135 closes the deficit by cutting wants, not needs.

misconceptions.B: Cuts a need and creates fees

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Abby is paid $1,150 every two weeks (net). What is her average MONTHLY take-home pay?
questions.feedback: 26 paychecks × $1,150 = $29,900 per year ÷ 12 ≈ $2,491.67 per month. Budgeting on $2,300 is a safer, conservative choice.

misconceptions.A: Assumes exactly two paychecks every month

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Start a budget with net income
sections.relationship: Budgets fail when they start from gross pay; students must use take-home pay.

questions.prompt: Max's gross pay is $2,600 a month and his take-home pay is $2,080. Which amount should his budget start with?
questions.intro: Budgets start with take-home (net) pay, the money you actually receive. Gross pay includes taxes and deductions you never get to spend.
questions.feedback: Start with take-home pay: $2,080.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Max's gross pay is $2,600 a month and his take-home pay is $2,080. If he builds his budget on $2,600, what happens?

choices.text: He plans to spend $520 he never receives
He saves an extra $520 by accident
Nothing, because the bank adjusts it
His income taxes go down by $520 for the year

questions.correct_answer: He plans to spend $520 he never receives
questions.feedback: $2,600 − $2,080 = $520 of planned spending with no money behind it.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only items Max must plan for each month?

choices.text: Rent, food, transportation, and savings
Rent, a vacation, and a new laptop
Food, gifts, and concert tickets
Only rent, since everything else changes

questions.feedback: Regular needs and a savings line belong in every monthly plan.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Max's budget: income $2,080; expenses $1,900; savings $180. Is it balanced?

choices.text: No; it has a $180 surplus
No; it has a $180 deficit
No; savings should not be included in a budget
Yes; income equals spending plus saving

questions.correct_answer: Yes; income equals spending plus saving
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which tool can be used to keep a budget?

choices.text: Only an app from your bank
Only a paid financial advisor or planner
Only a tax return
A spreadsheet, an app, or a notebook

questions.correct_answer: A spreadsheet, an app, or a notebook
questions.feedback: Any tool works if you use it consistently.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Budget results subtract planned spending from income.

sections.skill: Interpret sums of rational numbers in context
sections.relationship: A deficit is a negative result that must be understood and fixed.

ref_skill.name: Interpret sums of rational numbers in real-world situations

questions.prompt: "Pay yourself first" means…

choices.text: saving first, as soon as you are paid
buying something fun for yourself on every payday
paying your own bills before your roommates pay theirs
saving only whatever is left at the end of the month

questions.correct_answer: saving first, as soon as you are paid
questions.intro: "Pay yourself first" treats saving like a bill: a set amount goes to savings right when income arrives, often by automatic transfer. Saving "whatever is left" often leaves nothing.
questions.feedback: Saving first, automatically, makes saving consistent.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Abby saves 10% of each $1,150 paycheck automatically. How much does she save in a year (26 paychecks)?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Why does automating savings help?

choices.text: It removes the need to decide every payday
Automatic transfers earn double the usual interest rate
Banks require automatic savings by law
It prevents all spending

questions.correct_answer: It removes the need to decide every payday
questions.feedback: Automation turns saving into a habit that does not depend on willpower.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Abby's savings transfer is set for the day after payday. Why is that timing better than the day before payday?

choices.text: Transfers are free only after payday
Interest is paid only after payday
It makes no difference at all
Money is there to transfer, so it is less likely to cause an overdraft

questions.correct_answer: Money is there to transfer, so it is less likely to cause an overdraft
questions.feedback: Scheduling right after pay arrives avoids overdrafts and protects savings from spending.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Abby has $2,990 in savings, built by saving part of each paycheck. Her car needs a $400 repair. Which choice is wisest?

choices.text: Use savings, then rebuild them over the next months
Put the repair on a credit card and never pay it off
Skip the repair and drive an unsafe car
Stop saving forever because savings got used

questions.correct_answer: Use savings, then rebuild them over the next months
questions.feedback: Savings exist for needs like this; rebuilding keeps the habit.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: In the envelope method, cash for each category goes in its own envelope. What happens when the "eating out" envelope is empty?

choices.text: Money is borrowed from the rent envelope for now
A credit card covers the extra
The envelope refills automatically
Eating out stops until the next budget period

questions.correct_answer: Eating out stops until the next budget period
questions.intro: The envelope method sets a fixed amount for each spending category. When a category runs out, spending in it stops. Many apps copy this idea digitally.
questions.feedback: The method works by stopping spending when a category's money is used up.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A budgeting app shows Sam spent $260 of a $300 grocery budget with 8 days left in the month. About how much can he spend per day for groceries for the rest of the month?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which method plans to spend EVERY dollar of income on a purpose?

choices.text: A zero-based budget
Spending freely and checking the balance
Saving whatever is left at month end
Paying only the minimums on all bills

questions.feedback: Zero-based budgets assign every dollar.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which situation shows a budget that needs revising?

choices.text: One unusual month with a holiday gift
Spending matches the plan
A surplus that is saved
Spending is over budget in the same categories every month

questions.correct_answer: Spending is over budget in the same categories every month
questions.feedback: Repeated overspending means the plan is unrealistic and should be changed.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Sam's grocery budget is $300, but he has spent $360, $350, and $370 in the last three months. What is the most realistic revised budget, based on his average?
questions.feedback: Average: ($360 + $350 + $370) ÷ 3 = $360. He should budget about $360 or find real ways to spend less.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
